name: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
description: Two labeled subsets of the 80 million tiny images dataset. CIFAR-10 contains 6000 images in each of 10 classes (airplane, automobile, bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship, truck). CIFAR-100 contains 600 images in each of 100 non-overlapping classes organized into 20 superclasses. Images are 32x32 color images collected from the web.
creator: Alex Krizhevsky
citeAs: Alex Krizhevsky. Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images. April 8, 2009.
rai:dataCollection: The tiny images dataset was collected by colleagues at MIT and NYU over the span of six months by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in the lexical database WordNet. They used several search engines, including Google, Flickr, and AltaVista and kept roughly the first 3000 results for each search term. After collecting all the images for a particular search term, they removed perfect duplicates and images in which an excessively large portion of the pixels were white. The dataset contains 80 million color images downscaled to 32x32 and spread out across 79000 search terms.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images were collected from the web using search engines (Google, Flickr, AltaVista) by searching for every non-abstract English noun in WordNet. Roughly the first 3000 results for each search term were kept.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Perfect duplicates were removed. Images in which an excessively large portion of the pixels were white were removed as they tended to be synthetic figures rather than natural images. All images were downscaled to 32x32 pixels. Duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm and using a rejection threshold liberal enough to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were downscaled to 32x32 pixels. A whitening transformation (ZCA whitening) was applied to some experiments, which decorrelates data dimensions. The 1000 least-significant directions of variance were deleted from the dataset. For some experiments, data was normalized by setting the standard deviation of visible units.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Students were paid to label a subset of the tiny images dataset. Labelers were given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term, including hyponyms from WordNet. Labelers were instructed to reject images that did not belong to their assigned class based on specific criteria: (1) The class name should be high on the list of likely answers to 'What is in this picture?', (2) The image should be photo-realistic (line drawings rejected), (3) The image should contain only one prominent instance of the object, (4) The object may be partially occluded or seen from an unusual viewpoint as long as its identity is still clear. Every label submitted by labelers was personally verified.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Every label submitted by the labelers was personally verified by the researchers. The criteria emphasized that false positives (incorrectly including an image) are worse than false negatives (incorrectly excluding an image).
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The CIFAR-100 dataset includes a 'people' superclass with classes: baby, boy, girl, man, woman, which may contain images of human subjects with potentially identifiable characteristics.
rai:dataBiases: The search term used to find an image provides it with a rough label, although it is extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology. Images tend to be symmetric about the vertical and horizontal, probably caused by the way people take photographs - making the ground plane horizontal and centering on the main object. The dataset reflects biases inherent in web image search results and photographer composition preferences.
rai:dataLimitations: The original tiny images dataset has extremely unreliable labels due to the nature of online image search technology. The labeled subsets (CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100) were created to address this limitation. Images are limited to 32x32 resolution. The dataset may contain near-duplicates despite efforts to remove them. The classes in CIFAR-10 have specific exclusions (e.g., automobile excludes trucks and pickup trucks; truck excludes pickup trucks).
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset was divided into training and test sets, with the training set receiving a randomly-selected 5000 images from each class (for CIFAR-10). The dataset is used for: (1) Unsupervised training of deep generative models, (2) Object classification experiments, (3) Pre-training features for object recognition, (4) Training and evaluating feed-forward neural networks. The paper demonstrates that object recognition is significantly improved by pre-training a layer of features on a large set of unlabeled tiny images.
